METADATA.title: Vintage Fender Jaguar Value Guide: 1962 To 1975 Prices
METADATA.description: Vintage Fender Jaguar values for every year from 1962 to 1975, with dated sale comparisons, original finish, repairs, cases and photos from my archive.

OUTLINE: ## Vintage Fender Jaguar Values By Year
### Later Jaguars And The Player Market
## Original Finish And Custom Color Value
## Asking Price, Sale Price And Your Proceeds
## Getting A Value For Your Jaguar
BODY:
Vintage Fender Jaguar sunburst comparisons run from $3,700 to $10,000 across the original 1962 to 1975 production years, with the condition and case differences set out below. First-year examples sit at $6,300 to $10,000 in this sample; the 1970s comparison is $3,700 to $4,500. I use those as starting comparisons, then account for the exact guitar rather than treating every example as equally complete.

I start with the guitar's year and configuration, then compare the finish, parts, repairs and case with the instruments behind the range. If you need to establish the year or originality first, my [vintage Fender Jaguar authentication guide](/post/vintage-fender-jaguar-guide/) explains the evidence to check.

## Vintage Fender Jaguar Values By Year

As of October 2026, the table uses three independent completed Reverb transactions for each era comparison. The 1965 row preserves this site's existing $4,000 to $6,000 conditional reference; three verified sales fall inside it. Amounts are in U.S. dollars, excluding separately charged shipping and taxes. Each row names the year, but repeated ranges share an era sample rather than a separate set of same-year sales.

| Year | Sunburst Comparison | Basis And Condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1962 | $6,300 to $10,000 | First-year sample, Very Good to Excellent; case and originality documentation vary |
| 1963 | $5,900 to $6,800 | 1963 to 1964 era, Very Good; see parts and case allowances |
| 1964 | $5,900 to $6,800 | 1963 to 1964 era, Very Good; see parts and case allowances |
| 1965 | $4,000 to $6,000 | Existing conditional reference, checked against completed sunburst sales |
| 1966 | $4,000 to $4,500 | 1966 to 1969 era, Very Good originals with original cases |
| 1967 | $4,000 to $4,500 | 1966 to 1969 era, Very Good originals with original cases |
| 1968 | $4,000 to $4,500 | 1966 to 1969 era, Very Good originals with original cases |
| 1969 | $4,000 to $4,500 | 1966 to 1969 era, Very Good originals with original cases |
| 1970 | $3,700 to $4,500 | 1970 to 1975 era, Excellent; see case and service allowances |
| 1971 | $3,700 to $4,500 | 1970 to 1975 era, Excellent; see case and service allowances |
| 1972 | $3,700 to $4,500 | 1970 to 1975 era, Excellent; see case and service allowances |
| 1973 | $3,700 to $4,500 | 1970 to 1975 era, Excellent; see case and service allowances |
| 1974 | $3,700 to $4,500 | 1970 to 1975 era, Excellent; see case and service allowances |
| 1975 | $3,700 to $4,500 | 1970 to 1975 era, Excellent; see case and service allowances |

The first-year range mixes examples with different levels of documentation and includes a replacement case and replacement mute foam. It isn't a separate slab-board premium or a promise of museum condition. The 1963 to 1964 comparison allows missing accessories, a replacement case and fretwork; the three documented instruments are from 1963.

The 1965 reference accommodates transition features and differing condition. One completed comparison needs fretwork, and the sample doesn't consistently establish original-case completeness. The late-1960s comparison covers original sunburst guitars with original cases, visible wear and no disclosed structural repair; it includes 1966 and 1969 instruments.

The 1970s comparison draws on 1971 and 1972 rosewood-board instruments. Two are described as completely original with original cases; the third documents original pickups and includes a molded case without a complete originality inventory. One original example has a disclosed grounding issue. The remaining 1970s rows use that same era evidence, so an unusually clean, fully documented guitar may need a narrower appraisal.

These aren't custom-color, maple-board, refinished or heavily modified price bands. I haven't converted those categories into a fixed premium or discount. The dated source record keeps each completed transaction and its condition notes available for review.

The original Jaguar run ends in 1975. A guitar described as a 1976, 1977, 1978 or 1979 Jaguar needs its identity checked before you apply an original-run price. A date on a receipt, a replacement part or a later reissue name doesn't establish its manufacturing year.

[IMAGE 1]

## Choosing The Right Comparison

A price range is useful only when the guitar behind it resembles yours. A sunburst Jaguar with its original pickups, original finish and a serviceable case belongs in a different comparison from a refinished guitar with changed electronics. They can both be good instruments, but a buyer is purchasing a different package.

The annual rows make the guide easier to use when you know a year. They don't imply that a guitar gained a fixed amount of value when the calendar changed. Where adjacent years share a range, they're using the same era evidence. A small sample doesn't justify inventing a separate price for every serial-number window.

I also distinguish the condition grade printed on a listing from a description of the actual parts. “Excellent” can describe a clean refinished guitar, while “Very Good” can describe an original guitar with visible playing wear. Neither label, by itself, establishes an original finish, an untouched wiring harness or the right case.

The same distinction applies to maintenance. A quality refret is accepted maintenance and preserves the all-original classification of an otherwise all-original guitar. It removes the instrument from the museum-quality category. Neck reshaping, a replacement fingerboard and enlarged tuner holes are different alterations and need their own assessment.

### The First-Year Question

The Jaguar arrived in 1962, and first-year instruments deserve a closer comparison than a generic “pre-CBS Fender” description. Early slab-board and later veneer-board guitars belong to that same calendar year. Slab and veneer describe two different rosewood fingerboard constructions; they aren't condition grades.

The first-year price evidence here doesn't establish a separate slab-board premium. I won't apply a later-1962 result to an exceptional early example without checking that distinction. Nor will I assume that a guitar is early production because its owner remembers buying it soon after the model appeared.

A first-year guitar also needs its finish separated from its year. A standard sunburst comparison can't price an authenticated rare custom color. That doesn't make every unusual-looking color valuable: the premium depends on the finish actually being original and on finding comparable demand for that configuration.

### Why 1965 Needs Its Own Context

The CBS purchase happened in 1965, but the instruments didn't change all at once. A 1965 Jaguar can retain earlier features or show later changes. The earlier guide's conditional value reference is retained in the notes rather than treated as proof that every guitar from that year is interchangeable.

For an appraisal, I want the actual configuration described alongside the year. A seller's “pre-CBS” label isn't a substitute for that description. Once the guitar is identified, the comparison can account for its features without assigning a premium to a slogan.

### Later Jaguars And The Player Market

Late-1960s and 1970s Jaguars have their own buyers. Some want a vintage instrument they can use regularly; others collect a particular finish, fingerboard or period. A later guitar doesn't need to imitate a first-year example to have a market.

For these instruments, comfortable setup, working electronics and disclosed modifications help a buyer understand the package. A guitar with missing parts or unresolved playing problems may need a different comparison even when the finish looks clean. A repair estimate should come from inspecting the problem, not from subtracting a generic percentage.

[IMAGE 2]

## Original Finish And Custom Color Value

An original finish is part of the collectible instrument. Repainting changes that category even when the new work looks attractive and the guitar plays well. I compare a refinished Jaguar with other refinished examples instead of assuming that a new coat of a rare color recreates the rare original.

Custom colors need separate evidence. A few expensive advertisements don't establish a completed-sale range, and the premium for one color doesn't automatically transfer to another. I haven't added an unsupported percentage to the sunburst rows to manufacture a custom-color table.

If the finish is the unresolved part of your guitar's story, the [Fender custom color authentication guide](/post/fender-custom-color-authentication-guide/) covers the finish evidence. Here, the value question starts after that identification is settled. The buyer needs to know which finish they're paying for.

Normal aging can change how a finish looks without making it a refinish. I describe the visible color and wear separately from the conclusion about originality. A photograph with warm lighting isn't enough to establish the factory color, and a polished surface isn't evidence that a guitar has escaped repair.

Wear also needs context. The edges, back and areas touched while playing may show use on an otherwise original guitar. A large repair, added routing or changed finish is a different issue from worn lacquer. I don't combine all of them under a vague “player grade” label and leave a buyer to guess.

[IMAGE 3]

## Condition, Repairs And Replacement Parts

The price table is a starting comparison, not a list of automatic deductions. Two Jaguars can have the same replacement part and different values because the work affected them differently. A bridge that can be exchanged without changing the body is a different proposition from an enlarged pickup cavity.

Original pickups and electronics help define the guitar. If a pickup has been replaced, I want to know whether the original survives and whether it works. A box containing an original component can improve the completeness of the package, but it doesn't make an undocumented alteration disappear.

A changed switch or potentiometer also needs a plain description. A potentiometer is the electrical control behind a volume or tone knob. Replacing one may have been necessary maintenance; the buyer still needs to know what changed and whether the older part comes with the instrument.

Structural repairs require more detail than “professionally repaired.” The location, extent and present stability of the repair affect the comparison. Photographs and any repair paperwork help, but the final assessment may need an in-person inspection. I don't assign the same discount to every repaired neck or every filled screw hole.

The playing condition belongs in the appraisal too. A neck that won't adjust as expected, worn frets, intermittent switches or a bridge that needs attention can change what a buyer is willing to take on. Tell me about those issues before commissioning work purely to prepare the guitar for sale.

### Refretting And Originality

A quality refret can make a vintage Jaguar easier to use while preserving the all-original classification of an otherwise original instrument. That classification is separate from museum-quality condition. An instrument can be collectible and useful without retaining unusable frets.

The appraisal still considers the quality and extent of the work. Refretting doesn't authorize reshaping the neck or altering the fingerboard. If those changes accompanied the fret work, they should be disclosed separately rather than hidden inside the word “refret.”

[IMAGE 4]

## Hardware, Mute And Case Completeness

The Jaguar's hardware is part of the package being compared. Record the bridge, tremolo arm, covers and other included pieces before you move anything. If a replacement is fitted and an older part survives in the case, photograph both and explain which is which.

The Jaguar mute is the hinged plate behind the bridge with a thumb lever and a foam pad. Its foam deteriorates over time, so intact original foam is a collector find. A fresh foam pad should be described as replacement material, and the mute assembly should be described on its own merits.

The case needs the same specificity. “Comes with a case” doesn't tell a buyer whether it's the original case, a period replacement or a modern hard case. A modern case can be useful for transport while remaining a different collectible package from an original case with its accessories.

Save the small items. A tremolo arm, original bridge, instruction sheet, hang tag or dated receipt can help document what accompanies the guitar. I don't add a fixed dollar premium for a bundle whose contents and condition haven't been checked. Instead, I describe the package and compare it with similarly complete instruments.

[IMAGE 5]

## Asking Price, Sale Price And Your Proceeds

A dealer's asking price is an invitation to buy. A completed price records a transaction. Your proceeds are what remains after the costs and terms of your chosen sale. Those figures can differ without any of them being dishonest.

The completed comparisons in this guide use the recorded final transaction amount rather than the last advertisement shown on a listing. I check the accompanying description because a bargain-looking number may belong to a refinish, replacement pickups, a repair or an incomplete guitar. A listing that merely ended doesn't independently prove a sale.

The date of the comparison is also part of the evidence. An older result can provide context, but it doesn't establish today's price by itself. I haven't applied an automatic inflation multiplier or assumed that every vintage Jaguar has appreciated at the same rate.

For a private sale, you also need to weigh the time spent answering questions, arranging payment, packing and resolving a buyer's concerns. A dealer offer is a separate proposal with its own terms. Neither should be confused with an upper-end retail asking price pulled from an unrelated guitar.

An appraisal can narrow the comparison once the guitar is documented. It isn't a promise that a particular buyer will pay the top of a range on a particular day. Unusual finishes, substantial repairs and mixed original parts are the cases where a broad online table needs the most individual work.

[IMAGE 6]

## Getting A Value For Your Jaguar

Start with photographs of the full front and back, the headstock, the case and any known repairs or replacement parts. Include the year you believe it is and the history you actually know. If you aren't sure about a finish or component, say so; uncertainty is useful information.

You don't need to take the guitar apart for an initial conversation. Existing photographs of hidden dates or components are helpful if you already have them. I can explain what additional evidence is needed after looking at the complete instrument.

Keep the original parts, paperwork and case together. Don't repaint the guitar, enlarge a cavity or discard old hardware to make the package look newer before asking about value. If it already has modifications, describe them plainly and we can use the appropriate comparison.

I buy vintage guitars nationwide from my shop in Mesa. You can request a [free Jaguar appraisal](/free-appraisal/) with photographs, or read about [selling a vintage Fender guitar](/sell-my-fender-guitar/) if you're ready to discuss a sale. I'll use the guitar in front of us, its documentation and the available market evidence to explain the range that fits.

mainEntity.name: What Is A 1965 Fender Jaguar Worth?

acceptedAnswer.text: This guide retains the site's existing $4,000 to $6,000 conditional reference for 1965. Three verified completed sunburst sales fall within it, but their condition and case completeness vary. I check the actual transition features, original finish, pickups and required work before applying that reference.

mainEntity.name: Does Every Annual Row Have Its Own Sale Sample?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Adjacent years can share an explicitly labeled era comparison. The 1963 and 1964 rows use the same early veneer-board sample, and the later groups work the same way. I haven't invented annual premiums where the evidence only supports an era range.

mainEntity.name: Does An Original Custom Color Have A Fixed Premium?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The color, originality, condition and available completed comparisons determine the premium. A rare-color asking price doesn't establish what an ordinary sunburst or a refinished guitar will bring.

mainEntity.name: How Does A Refinish Affect Jaguar Value?

acceptedAnswer.text: A refinish changes the collector comparison, even if the work is attractive and the guitar plays well. I compare it with other refinished examples and account separately for routing, repairs and changed parts. There isn't one percentage that describes every guitar.

mainEntity.name: Does A Quality Refret Change The Originality Category?

acceptedAnswer.text: A quality refret is accepted maintenance and preserves the all-original classification of an otherwise all-original guitar. It takes the instrument out of the museum-quality category. Neck reshaping and fingerboard alterations are separate changes.

mainEntity.name: Is A Dealer Offer The Same As The Table Price?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The table is a market comparison with stated conditions. A purchase offer has its own terms, while a private seller's proceeds depend on fees, shipping, repairs and the final agreement. I explain the comparison and the proposed offer separately.

Frequently Asked Questions

### Which Vintage Fender Jaguar Years Are Worth the Most? 1962 Jaguars in original condition with slab rosewood fingerboards, intact mute systems, and especially custom color finishes command the highest valuations. A clean 1962 in Fiesta Red, Sonic Blue, or Olympic White with full original case candy can reach figures well above standard sunburst examples of the same year. After that, the entire pre-CBS run from 1962 through early 1965 sits in the top tier, with 1963 examples being the most commonly traded since 1962 production was smaller. ### How Much Does a Refinish Reduce a Vintage Jaguar's Value? A professional, well documented refinish in a period correct color typically reduces value by 40 to 60 percent compared to an original finish guitar of the same year and condition. A poorly executed or non period correct refinish can drop value by 70 percent or more. The reasoning is straightforward: an original finish guitar is unrepeatable, while a refinish puts the instrument in the same value tier as a thousand other refinished Jaguars on the market. ### Do Replacement Pickups Hurt the Value? Yes, but the impact depends on whether the originals are present and whether the replacement was professional. If the original pickups come with the guitar (kept aside while modern replacements were installed for playability), the value impact is minimal. If the originals are gone and the guitar has been routed for humbuckers or other non-standard pickups, the impact is severe because the body modification is permanent and visible. Standard single coil replacements that fit the original routes without modification reduce value but the guitar remains marketable. ### Is a 1965 Fender Jaguar Pre-CBS or CBS? 1965 was a strong production year. Several thousand Jaguars left the factory that year, more than 1962 and 1963 combined. What matters within 1965 is whether the guitar wears pre-CBS specs or full CBS specs. Early to mid 1965 instruments with clay or pearloid dot inlays, unbound rosewood fingerboards, and 4 ply nitrate pickguards are pre-CBS in character even though CBS owned the company. Late 1965 instruments with bound fingerboards, pearloid blocks, and 3 ply pickguards are fully CBS. The gold transition logo runs across both halves of 1965 (the Jaguar never wore a spaghetti logo), so the dating distinction has to come from the inlay style, fingerboard binding, pickguard material, and pot codes rather than the headstock decal. The price difference between these two "1965" categories is significant. ### How Can I Tell Whether a Custom Color Is Original? Pull the neck and pull the pickguard. A factory original custom color shows you four things at once: a paint stick shadow in the neck pocket (on guitars from late 1962 on, where the wooden stick that held the body during spraying left an un-colored shadow inside the pocket), clean unpainted Fender nail holes under the pickguard and bridge (on 1962 to 1964 guitars), a yellowish amber Fullerplast layer visible at chips and cavity edges, and a color that matches a documented Fender catalog spec for the claimed year. A refinish usually misses on one or more: sunburst peeking through under the pickguard, no paint stick shadow in the pocket, painted-over nail holes, no Fullerplast under the color, or a hue that does not match any catalog spec. A color that was never in the period catalog is an immediate red flag. ### What Does the Jaguar's Strangle Switch Do? The strangle switch is the third slider on the lower bout control plate. Engaging it routes the signal through a 0.003 microfarad capacitor in series, which aggressively rolls off the bass frequencies. The result is a thin, brittle, treble-heavy tone that Fender originally marketed as a "low cut" or "filtered" sound. Most players never use it. Verifying that the switch and its associated cap are original is a small originality check but worth doing on a collector grade instrument. ### Did Vintage Jaguars Ever Use a Three-Bolt Neck? No. Unlike the Stratocaster and Telecaster which moved to three bolt neck plates with the bullet truss rod in the early 1970s, the Jaguar retained its four bolt neck and heel adjusted truss rod throughout its entire 1962 to 1975 production run. Any Jaguar with a three bolt neck has been modified or assembled from non-original parts. This is a useful authentication shortcut. ### What Case Should an Original Jaguar Have? The original case styles followed Fender's broader case program. 1962 Jaguars shipped in brown Tolex covered cases with orange or pink plush interiors. By the mid 1960s the case shifted to black Tolex with orange plush, then to black Tolex with various interior colors through the late 60s and 70s. An original-to-the-guitar case adds value, and case candy (the original warranty card, hangtags, polish cloth, tremolo arm, mute foam) adds more. ### Are 1970s Fender Jaguars Worth Buying? Yes, particularly as players. The 1970s Jaguars sell at much lower prices than their pre-CBS counterparts and many of them play and sound excellent. The instruments suffer from polyester finishes that feel different than nitrocellulose and from less consistent fretwork, but the basic Jaguar circuit and pickups remained intact through the entire production run. For a working musician who wants a real vintage Fender Jaguar without paying pre-CBS money, a clean 1973 or 1974 example can be a strong purchase. ### How Does Jaguar Scale Length Compare With a Jazzmaster? The Fender Jaguar has a 24 inch scale length, while the Fender Jazzmaster has a 25.5 inch scale (the standard Fender length shared with the Stratocaster and Telecaster). That 1.5 inch difference is felt immediately when you switch between them. The Jaguar's shorter scale means lower string tension at the same gauge, easier bends, and a more compact reach across the frets. It also means that light gauge strings can feel floppy on a Jaguar, which is one of the reasons the model has so many bridge buzz issues with modern setups. Most experienced Jaguar players use 11 gauge or heavier strings to maintain tension. If you are choosing between the two models for purchase, the Jaguar is the shorter scale, brighter pickup, more complex switching option, while the Jazzmaster is the standard scale, warmer pickup, simpler switching option. ### Do a Buzz Stop or Replacement Bridge Hurt Collector Value? A standard **Buzz Stop** fits under the two existing front tremolo screws and does not require drilling, so it is normally reversible. **Mastery** and **Staytrem** bridges can also be reversible when the correct model drops into the factory thimbles. Value concerns begin when an installation adds holes, replaces or enlarges the original thimbles, or separates the guitar from its factory bridge. Check the actual installation rather than assuming the brand name alone proves damage. ### What Are the Small Nail Holes Under an Early Jaguar's Pickguard? Before late 1964, Fender's painting process used small nails driven into the body to suspend it during spraying. The nails went into spots that would be hidden under the pickguard or under the bridge after assembly. The result is small clean unpainted holes in the wood of every pre-late-1964 original finish body. When a body is refinished, those nail holes get filled with paint or sanded smooth and refilled, so an original finish 1962 to 1964 Jaguar will have clean unpainted nail holes under the pickguard and around the bridge area, while a refinished body of the same era will show the holes filled with paint or missing entirely. This is one of the most reliable refinish detection methods on a pre-1965 Fender and one of the first things a serious buyer checks. ### Can I Date a Vintage Jaguar From the Serial Number Alone? No, and this is one of the most common mistakes we see. Fender stamped neck plates in batches and pulled them from bins as guitars came together, so plates were not used in strict sequential order. A 1963 L-series plate can appear on a guitar actually built in 1964, and a serial number lookup against any chart will give you a range of two or three possible years rather than a single answer. Worse, the plate itself is just four screws away from being installed on a different guitar, which is exactly how parts assembled "vintage" Jaguars get built and sold. The only reliable date comes from triangulating the neck stamp, body date, pot codes, pickup bottom color, and feature set together. That is exactly the kind of inspection we provide as part of a free appraisal. ### Where Can I Get a Vintage Fender Jaguar Appraised? The fastest path is a hands-on inspection by a dealer who specializes in vintage Fenders. Photos and serial number lookups are a useful first pass, but the triangulation of neck date, body date, pot codes, pickup construction, brass shielding, Fullerplast layer, and feature consistency cannot be fully done from photographs. We provide free **vintage guitar appraisals** on Jaguars and other vintage Fenders, with cash offers extended on authentic original examples. [Reach out for a free appraisal here](/free-appraisal/), or if you have already decided to [sell a vintage Fender Jaguar](/free-appraisal/), send us the photos and the details from this guide and we will get you a real number.

Jaguar Authentication Questions

### Can I Date A Vintage Jaguar From The Serial Number Alone? No. Fender neck plates came from shared bins and their ranges overlap. I compare the neck stamp, body date, potentiometer codes, pickup construction, hardware and feature set before assigning a year. ### Is A 1965 Fender Jaguar Pre-CBS Or CBS? The calendar alone isn't enough. Earlier features overlap the CBS ownership period, and later guitars show changes such as fingerboard binding and a different pickguard. I compare the actual neck, guard, hardware, dates and electronics rather than relying on the seller's label. ### Does The Headstock Decal Sit Under The Clear Coat? No. The water-slide decal goes on top of the finished clear coat, last. A decal buried under lacquer indicates a respray in the wrong order. Dealer and shop decals also sit on top of the finish. ### Is Fullerplast The Yellow Material In A Cavity? Fullerplast is colorless. The yellow visible in pockets and cavities comes from the aniline dye stain applied before the sealer. I don't treat yellow color alone as proof of a factory finish. ### What Should I Expect From The Jaguar Mute? The Jaguar mute is a hinged plate behind the bridge with a thumb lever and foam pad. The foam deteriorates with age, so intact original foam is a collector find. The Jazzmaster didn't use this fitting. ### Did Vintage Jaguars Use A Three-Bolt Neck? No. The original Jaguar run kept a four-bolt neck and heel-adjusted truss rod. A three-bolt attachment on a guitar presented as an original vintage Jaguar needs investigation for modification or a parts assembly. ### Where Is The Jaguar Body Date? The body date is stamped in the tremolo cavity under the tremolo plate, or under the pickguard. It isn't in the neck pocket: the stamp people read there belongs to the neck heel. ### What Do Paint-Stick And Nail Marks Tell Me? Fender adopted the paint stick around December 1962 while still using face nails for horizontal drying racks until late 1964. A factory 1963 to early-1964 body shows both a stick shadow and open nail holes. A 1963 body with a stick shadow but no nail holes is a refinish warning.

changes.remove: Get one thing straight before you go looking for it, because it is misstated constantly: Fullerplast itself is transparent and colorless. The yellow-amber you see in neck pockets and cavities is the aniline dye stain Fender dipped the body in, sitting under the clear sealer. What you are reading is that stain-and-sealer layer, not a coloured sealer. It does not react to standard nitrocellulose solvents the way bare wood does, and under UV light it fluoresces in a recognizable pattern. Pull the pickguard on any factory original 1963 to 1975 Jaguar and you will see Fullerplast under the routing edges, in the pickup cavity walls, and at any small chip in the topcoat. A guitar that has been stripped and resprayed will not have it (you cannot reproduce Fullerplast in a home shop), and the absence of that yellow amber sealer beneath the color coat is the cleanest refinish tell on the instrument.

changes.remove: The easiest places to inspect are the lower pickup cavity walls (with the pickguard off and pickup removed), the neck pocket walls and floor, and any small finish chip on the body edge. You are looking for that glassy dye-stained surface under clear sealer, sitting between the bare wood and the topcoat color. On a sunburst body it sits beneath the yellow center and is sometimes hard to distinguish from the yellow itself, so the cleanest read is on a custom color body where it sits between the alder and the custom color paint. No Fullerplast means refinished, full stop, on any 1963 or later Jaguar.
changes.replaceWith: Inspect exposed finish layers at existing chips and accessible cavity edges without scraping or removing material. Separate the stain, clear sealer and color coat in your notes. The other dated parts and finish evidence still need to agree.
changes.reason: Correct conflict with supplied Fender finish/decal house rulings.

changes.remove: The decal sits under the clear coat. On an original guitar, the gold or black ink lies beneath the lacquer or polyester layer and you can sometimes feel the slight texture of the decal edge if you run a fingernail very gently across it from a low angle. A modern reproduction decal applied on top of the finish (which is how counterfeiters and home-refinishers work) sits on the surface, has crisper edges, and often shows a slightly different ink color than the period correct version. Black light inspection helps too: an aged original decal fluoresces differently than a fresh reproduction.
changes.replaceWith: The water-slide decal goes on top of the clear coat, last. The order is maple, sealer, opaque color where present, clear nitro and then the decal. A decal buried under lacquer indicates a respray in the wrong order; dealer and shop decals also sit on top of the finish.
changes.reason: Correct conflict with supplied Fender finish/decal house rulings.

changes.remove: The **Fullerplast layer** is the clear chemically cured sealer applied to bare alder before any color goes on. It dyes the wood a yellowish amber tone, which is what you see when you look at a chip on a custom color body or into the pickup cavities of a finished guitar. This yellow appearance is the wood under the Fullerplast, not an undercoat. The Fullerplast itself is essentially clear.
changes.replaceWith: The **Fullerplast layer** is a colorless, chemically cured sealer. Yellow in pockets and cavities is the aniline dye stain beneath it, not dye produced by the sealer. Fender used Sherwin-Williams Homoclad from 1955 to about mid-1962.
changes.reason: Correct conflict with supplied Fender finish/decal house rulings.

changes.remove: This matters because amateur refinishers and parts builders often assume there is a standard "yellow undercoat" beneath every Fender custom color (because they have heard about the Fullerplast and confused it with a primer). A refinish that tries to reproduce a "yellow undercoat" beneath a custom color is wrong from the start. The actual factory process produced the yellow tone through the Fullerplast layer on the bare wood, not through a colored undercoat above it.
changes.replaceWith: There isn't a universal yellow primer beneath every Fender custom color. The yellow stain lies below the clear sealer; a colored primer or base coat, when used, is a different layer above it.
changes.reason: Correct conflict with supplied Fender finish/decal house rulings.

changes.remove: **3\. Fullerplast layer visible at chips and cavities.** Look for the yellowish amber sealer in pickup cavities, neck pocket walls, and any finish chip on the body edge. The Fullerplast sits between the wood and the color coat. No Fullerplast on a 1963 or later guitar means refinished, regardless of color.
changes.replaceWith: **3\. Stain, Sealer And Color Layers.** Fullerplast is colorless, and the yellow beneath it is aniline stain. Examine the layers alongside the nail holes, paint-stick shadow, wear and dated parts; yellow alone doesn't establish originality.
changes.reason: Correct conflict with supplied Fender finish/decal house rulings.
